doc.title: Derrick Gardner interviewed by Monk Rowe, Clinton, New York, May 9, 2013

title: Whether music has to mean something; moving the audience
summary: Gardner says concert music must engage and move listeners, comparing functional music with composed music.

story.theme_name: Where jazz stands today: young players, rock, and the audience
story.community_name: Playing for the audience: communicating from the bandstand

blocks.x: Well it kind of brings me to a question and I’m not sure how to ask it. But does music for you, or especially in your own compositions, does it have to mean something? Does it have to have a subtext or can it just be music?

I think that there is music that can be written to be functional, you know, that serves a purpose. Like I was just talking to Doc Woods about this earlier today. He was talking about writing for films. And the music has to convey a mood and not take away from the dialogue that’s being conveyed in the film. Or background music at a restaurant, you know, it serves a purpose. But when you’re composing music to be really listened to, concertized music, or even when you’re improvising, I’m one that believes that you have to move people you know, and you have to give your listeners something that’s going to keep that person engaged the entire time, or dialed in you know. And in that respect I do believe that music has to mean something. You know there are certain techniques that people use that can, you can say okay well I’m going to write what’s called a contrafact over “All the Things You Are.” You know you erase the melody, the chord changes are still there, and you just write a new melody. Okay, simple enough. Even when you’re doing that, that melody has to mean something. You know like Kenny Dorham did that with “All the Things You Are.” He wrote — well now I can’t think of the name of the tune — [scats]. Oh I can’t think of it. I’m sure that whoever listens to this, everyone probably knows it. But when I listen to that, that’s not music that I would listen to as like background music or elevator music or something. That music is engaging. And so that’s what I try to do every time I perform, I try to engage my listener. And every time I write I try to engage my listener in the same way that I improvise, I try to convey that on the score paper when I’m writing. And there are certain ways that you do that, manipulate the voicings or the tension. I always try to move people.

I had to chuckle because I read a quote of yours and it was almost exactly a quote that I got from Ed Shaughnessy years ago, and it was about if you look out there and at least some of the people aren’t moving or tapping your feet, you’re not doing your job.
You’re not doing your job, that’s right. Yeah. Yeah, Basie said the same thing. That’s right. That’s right.
